answer:
Magnetism starts with moving electric charge. Every electron acts like a tiny magnet, mostly because of a quantum property called spin. In most materials the electrons point in random or opposing directions, so their tiny fields cancel out. In a permanent magnet they add up to a net field around the object [1][2]. In "ferromagnetic" metals like iron, nickel and cobalt, neighboring atoms tend to line up their electron spins. This creates small regions called magnetic domains, each of which acts like a tiny bar magnet [1]. In an ordinary piece of iron the domains point every which way, so overall it isn't magnetic. A nearby magnet makes the domains line up, and the ones pointing the right way grow, which is why iron gets pulled toward a magnet. If that alignment gets locked in, for example by heating and cooling the iron near another magnet, it becomes a permanent magnet [1].

Opposite poles attract and like poles repel. Poles always come in north–south pairs, and no one has ever found a lone magnetic pole [1]. Heat breaks the alignment: above a material's Curie temperature it can't stay magnetized. For iron that's about 770 °C [1]. Electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field too, and that's how electromagnets work. They're usually wrapped around an iron core to make them stronger, and they switch off when the current stops [1].
